identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Shree Somnath is described by its own trust as the first among the twelve Aadi Jyotirlingas of Shiva. Devotees associate the site with Soma, the moon deity, who is said in tradition to have worshipped Shiva at Prabhas to recover his lustre. The shore temple's repeated destruction and rebuilding has made it, for many pilgrims, as much a site of continuity as of worship.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Somnath Temple, located at Prabhas in Gujarat, is the first among the twelve Jyotirlingas—the holiest shrines dedicated to Lord Shiva. Positioned at the confluence of the Veraval River and the Arabian Sea, the temple holds immense spiritual significance in Hinduism. According to legend, Chandra (the Moon God) worshipped Shiva here, earning the site its sacred status.

The temple has been destroyed and rebuilt multiple times throughout history. The current structure was rebuilt in 1951 after independence, featuring exquisite stone carvings and Chalukya architectural style. It stands as a symbol of Hindu resilience and spiritual devotion, attracting millions of pilgrims and tourists annually.
narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple at Prabhas Patan has one of the most heavily documented destruction-and-rebuilding sequences of any Indian shrine. Wikipedia's survey of the record lists Mahmud of Ghazni's raid of 1026, Alauddin Khalji's invasion of 1299, and further damage in 1395 and 1451, followed by Aurangzeb's order of 1706; Gujarat Tourism gives the same broad sequence with the dates 1025-26, 1297, 1394 and 1706. Between these episodes the shrine was rebuilt, notably by Kumarapala in 1169 and by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore in the 1780s. Archaeologically the picture is more cautious: Prabhas is an anciently settled site, but the existence of a temple there in antiquity is not confirmed by excavation.

The present building is a post-Independence reconstruction. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, then Deputy Prime Minister, visited the ruins and ordered the rebuilding, laying the foundation stone on 12 November 1947. The Shree Somnath Trust records that President Rajendra Prasad performed the Pran-Pratishtha of the new temple on 11 May 1951. The structure was built in the Māru-Gurjara idiom of Hindu temple architecture on the original coastal site.
narrative.sthalaPuranam: The Shree Somnath Trust's own account holds that Shiva, though present everywhere, manifests specially in twelve places as Jyotirlingas, of which Somnath is the first. Gujarat Tourism records the associated tradition that the shrine was first built in gold by Somraj, the moon god, then rebuilt in silver by Ravana, in wood by Krishna and in stone by Bhimdev.

visitingInfo.entryRules: No entry fee. Footwear must be removed before entering; complimentary shoe storage is provided. Mobile phones, cameras and smartwatches may not be carried in and can be left in free lockers.
visitingInfo.photographyPolicy: Photography is strictly prohibited inside the temple; electronic devices including cameras must be deposited in the free lockers.
visitingInfo.prasadInfo: The trust operates an online prasad service via somnathprasad.com.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Confirm same-day darshan, aarti and light-and-sound timings with the Shree Somnath Trust on +91-9428214914 (listed as a 24x7 line) or gmsomnathtrust@gmail.com; the trust's site and Gujarat Tourism currently publish different hours.

openingHours.notes: Stated by the Shree Somnath Trust on both its FAQ and Pilgrim Facilities pages. Gujarat Tourism publishes 6:30 AM to 9:00 PM for the same temple; treat as unsettled and confirm with the trust.
